country.name: Germany
country.summary: Germany grows Riesling at the cold edge of the vine, between roughly 47 and 52 degrees north, so its finest vineyards are steep, south facing and set over a river that stores heat and throws light back up the slope. Thirteen quality regions, the Anbaugebiete, share one law: Qualitätswein from a named region, and above it Prädikatswein, whose six Prädikate rank the sugar in the grapes at picking, never the sweetness in the glass. Trocken, halbtrocken and the unofficial feinherb say how dry the wine is. The VDP, a growers' association, lays a Burgundian pyramid over the top: Gutswein, Ortswein, Erste Lage, Grosse Lage, with the dry Grosses Gewächs at the summit. Spätburgunder is Pinot Noir, and Germany is a serious red wine country as well as the home of the lightest great white wines in the world.
country.overview:
The Romans planted the Mosel around Trier, and the monasteries of the Rhine, Benedictine at Johannisberg and Cistercian at Eberbach, carried the vine through the Middle Ages. In the nineteenth century the Rhine's Rieslings fetched prices beside the great clarets; the sweet Liebfraumilch flood of the twentieth century undid that name, and the dry revival of the last forty years has rebuilt it. The vineyards run in a band across the south west: the Mosel with its Saar and Ruwer tributaries, the Rhine from the Rheingau down through Rheinhessen and the Pfalz, the Nahe between them, the little Ahr and the Mittelrhein to the north, Franken on the Main, the Hessische Bergstrasse, Württemberg and Baden in the south, and far to the east Saale-Unstrut and Sachsen, added at reunification in 1990.

The wine law of 1971 drew the regions, registered every vineyard as an Einzellage or bundled it into a Grosslage, and ranked wine by ripeness because ripeness was the scarce thing. Must weight is read in degrees Oechsle, the density of the juice above water; a Kabinett needs roughly seventy to eighty degrees depending on region and grape, a Trockenbeerenauslese 150. Qualitätswein may be chaptalised, Prädikatswein never, and every quality wine passes an official tasting and carries an AP number. Because the ladder measures picking sugar, a Spätlese can be fermented bone dry. The dryness words are a separate axis: trocken allows up to 4 grams of sugar a litre, or 9 when the acidity sits within 2 grams of it; halbtrocken up to 12, or 18 when the acidity is within 10 grams of it; lieblich up to 45; and feinherb, off dry, is a trade word the label uses without a legal limit.

The VDP, founded in 1910, classified its members' vineyards from 2002 and settled on a four step pyramid in 2012: Gutswein, Ortswein, Erste Lage and Grosse Lage. A dry wine from a Grosse Lage is a Grosses Gewächs, GG, with the eagle on the capsule; a sweet wine from the same site carries its Prädikat. The federal law amended in January 2021 moves the whole country the same way. Origin now climbs in four steps, Anbaugebiet, Region (the old Bereich and Grosslage, which must carry that word), Ort and Einzellage, and Erstes Gewächs and Grosses Gewächs become legal terms for dry wines from single vineyards, with yields capped at 60 hectolitres a hectare for the first and 50 for the second (a little more on steep slopes), a minimum natural ripeness, hand picking for the GG, and release no earlier than the year after harvest, reds later still. The origin steps bind in full from the 2026 vintage.

The exam leans on the ladder in order, the Mosel against the Rheingau, slate and river, Eiswein's method, the Pinot synonyms, Sekt, and the Grosslage trap: Piesporter Michelsberg and Niersteiner Gutes Domtal sound like vineyards and are districts.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.styles: The national grape: late ripening, acid holding, faithful to its site. Featherweight and sweet on the Mosel, dry and firm in the Rheingau, Pfalz and Rheinhessen, and the only grape for great Eiswein and TBA.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Labelled Spätburgunder: dry, oak aged reds in Baden, the Ahr, the Pfalz and at Assmannshausen, and a Blanc de Noir and Sekt base. Germany is one of the world's three largest Pinot Noir growers.

grapes.name: Müller-Thurgau
grapes.styles: Bred at Geisenheim in 1882, also sold as Rivaner: soft, floral, early drinking white in volume, and the base of much Liebfraumilch.

grapes.name: Silvaner
grapes.styles: Earthy, pear and hay, soft acid; dry in Franken's Bocksbeutel and across Rheinhessen, the spring wine for asparagus.

grapes.name: Dornfelder
grapes.styles: A 1955 crossing bred for colour: deep, soft, plummy red, dry or off dry, the volume red of Rheinhessen and the Pfalz.

grapes.name: Pinot Gris / Grigio
grapes.styles: Grauburgunder when dry, Ruländer in the old sweet style: round, nutty, pear and smoke, at its best in Baden's Kaiserstuhl and the Pfalz.

grapes.name: Pinot Blanc
grapes.styles: Weissburgunder: dry, creamy, apple and almond, often with a little oak; the quiet food white of Baden, the Pfalz and the Nahe.

grapes.name: Gewürztraminer
grapes.styles: Traminer or Gewürztraminer on a German label: perfumed, lychee and rose, dry or sweet in small plots of the Pfalz, Baden and Franken.

exam: Recite the six Prädikate in order and say what each measures: must weight at picking, never sweetness in the glass.
Know the three dryness words and their sugar limits, and that feinherb is a trade term with no number.
Hold the VDP pyramid and the GG against the legal Prädikat ladder: two systems, one bottle.
Name the thirteen Anbaugebiete and place the big five on a map: Mosel, Rheingau, Nahe, Rheinhessen, Pfalz.
Explain Eiswein's method and why it ranks beside Beerenauslese without botrytis.
Give the Pinot synonyms and Germany's standing as a Pinot Noir country.
Spot a Grosslage on a label and say what the 2021 law does to it.
traps: A Spätlese trocken is a ripe dry wine and a Kabinett can taste sweet: read the Prädikat as picking sugar, then look for the dryness word.
German Kabinett is a Prädikat; Austrian Kabinett is a near dry Qualitätswein category capped at 9 g/L of sugar, not a Prädikat. Same word, different ladder.
Grosse Lage is a vineyard rank; Grosses Gewächs is the dry wine from it; Grosslage, one letter away, is a collective district name.
Eiswein needs no botrytis and may not come from a freezer: the frost happens on the vine at minus 7 °C or colder.
Liebfraumilch is a style defined by law, lieblich and cheap, from four Rhine regions and never from the Mosel.
Qualitätswein may be chaptalised; the moment a Prädikat is on the label it may not.
Trocken on a Sekt label means 17 to 32 g/L, far sweeter than a still trocken wine's 9.

cards.b: Kabinett, Spätlese, Auslese, Beerenauslese, Eiswein, Trockenbeerenauslese: must weight at picking, rising. Eiswein shares BA's minimum but comes from frost, not botrytis.

cards.f: Trocken, halbtrocken, feinherb: the sugar limits
cards.b: Trocken: up to 4 g/L, or 9 when acid is within 2 g/L of sugar. Halbtrocken: up to 12, or 18 when acid is within 10 g/L of sugar. Feinherb: off dry, no legal limit.

cards.f: The VDP pyramid, bottom to top
cards.b: Gutswein (estate), Ortswein (village), Erste Lage, Grosse Lage. The dry Grosse Lage wine is Grosses Gewächs, GG; sweet wines from those sites carry a Prädikat.
Ahr, Mittelrhein, Mosel, Rheingau, Nahe, Rheinhessen, Pfalz, Hessische Bergstrasse, Franken, Württemberg, Baden, Saale-Unstrut, Sachsen.
Spätburgunder is Pinot Noir; Grauburgunder (Ruländer when sweet) is Pinot Gris; Weissburgunder is Pinot Blanc; Frühburgunder is an early ripening Pinot Noir mutation.
Einzellage: one registered vineyard. Grosslage: a collective name over many villages that reads like a vineyard; from the 2026 vintage it must carry the word Region.
Healthy grapes left on the vine, picked and pressed frozen at minus 7 °C or colder; the water stays behind as ice, and must weight reaches BA level without botrytis.
A lieblich Qualitätswein from Rheinhessen, Pfalz, Nahe or Rheingau, at least 70 per cent Riesling, Silvaner, Müller-Thurgau or Kerner, at least 18 g/L of sugar.
Sekt: sparkling from any EU base wine. Deutscher Sekt: German base wine. Sekt b.A.: one Anbaugebiet. Winzersekt: a grower's own grapes, traditional method, nine months on the lees.

cards.f: The 2021 wine law in one breath
cards.b: Origin in four steps, Anbaugebiet, Region, Ort, Einzellage; Grosslagen labelled Region; Erstes and Grosses Gewächs legal dry single vineyard terms; binding from the 2026 vintage.

questions.q: Which Prädikat sits immediately above Spätlese on the ladder?
questions.exp: The order is Kabinett, Spätlese, Auslese, Beerenauslese, Eiswein, Trockenbeerenauslese, ranked by must weight at picking; Kabinett sits below Spätlese, and Beerenauslese and Eiswein share a floor above Auslese.

questions.q: To what temperature must grapes freeze on the vine for Eiswein?
questions.exp: German law asks that the grapes be frozen when picked and pressed, and minus 7 °C or colder is the figure its courts and the German Wine Institute give, so that the water stays in the press as ice and the must reaches Beerenauslese weight without botrytis.

questions.q: Spätburgunder is the German name for which grape?
questions.exp: Spätburgunder, the late Burgundian, is Pinot Noir; Grauburgunder is Pinot Gris and Weissburgunder Pinot Blanc, and Germany is among the three largest Pinot Noir growers in the world.

questions.q: Which of these quality designations may be chaptalised?
questions.exp: A plain Qualitätswein may have sugar added before fermentation to raise alcohol; any wine carrying a Prädikat, from Kabinett up to Trockenbeerenauslese, may not.

questions.q: What does the VDP call a dry wine from one of its Grosse Lage vineyards?
questions.exp: Grosse Lage is the site's rank; the dry wine made from it is the Grosses Gewächs, GG, marked by the eagle on the capsule; a sweet wine from the same site carries its Prädikat.

questions.q: In which year did the wine law draw the modern German regions and register every Einzellage?
questions.exp: The 1971 law created the Anbaugebiete, the Einzellage and Grosslage registers and the Prädikat ladder as it stands; 2021 brought the origin pyramid that will reshape it from the 2026 vintage.

questions.q: Which of these label names is a Grosslage rather than a single vineyard?
questions.exp: Piesporter Michelsberg is a collective name over flat land around Piesport; the Sonnenuhr, the Doctor and the Scharzhofberg are registered single vineyards.

questions.q: How many grams of sugar per litre may a trocken still wine hold when its acidity is high enough?
questions.exp: Trocken is 4 g/L as a rule, but up to 9 g/L when the total acidity lies within 2 g/L of the sugar; halbtrocken runs to 12, or 18 when the acidity is within 10 g/L of the sugar.

regions.name: Ahr
regions.summary: The Ahr is a narrow valley running east into the Rhine south of Bonn, one of the smallest and most northerly of the thirteen regions and the one that grows red. Spätburgunder, Pinot Noir, fills about two thirds of its slopes, with Frühburgunder, its early ripening cousin, as the local speciality and a little Portugieser and Riesling behind. The upper valley is a slate and greywacke gorge that traps heat; the lower valley around Ahrweiler and Bad Neuenahr opens onto loess and loam. Once a source of pale, sweetish reds for day trippers, since the 1980s it has made dry, oak aged Pinot Noir of Burgundian ambition. Say it: AHR.

terroir.climate: Cool and northerly, at about 50.5 degrees north, but the valley is a sheltered canyon: the Eifel hills to the south and west keep rain off, the steep south facing walls catch the low sun and the dark rock gives back its heat at night. Summers are warm enough to ripen Pinot Noir fully on the best slopes; frost and a cold, wet September are the risks.
terroir.soils: Devonian slate and greywacke, broken and dark, in the upper valley from Altenahr through Mayschoss, Rech and Dernau; the slate warms fast and drains fast, so vines dig deep and yields stay small. Downstream the valley widens and loess, loam and gravel over the same rock take over around Ahrweiler, Bad Neuenahr and Heimersheim, giving rounder, earlier wines. Volcanic rock shows in patches, a memory of the Eifel.
terroir.topography: A gorge a few hundred metres wide for most of its length, with vineyards on steep terraces and walls above the river; the valley bends constantly, so the exposures swing from full south to east and west around every curve. Vines run from Altenahr in the west some 25 kilometres down to Heimersheim near the Rhine.
terroir.water: The Ahr itself, a small, fast river that flows east to join the Rhine between Remagen and Sinzig. It reflects light onto the slopes and moderates the air. In July 2021 it rose catastrophically and destroyed cellars, bridges and vineyards along the whole valley; the rebuilding has defined the region since.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Labelled Spätburgunder and about two thirds of the vineyard: dry, barrel aged, silky, red cherry and smoke on slate, with Burgundy as the model.

grapes.name: Frühburgunder
grapes.styles: Pinot Noir Précoce, an early ripening mutation rescued from near extinction here: softer, darker fruited and lower in acid than Spätburgunder, the valley's own speciality.

grapes.name: Portugieser
grapes.styles: Light, simple, pale reds and Weissherbst rosé for the valley's own tables.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.styles: A small crop on the slate, racy and often dry, proof that the valley is northern.

grapes.name: Dornfelder
grapes.styles: A little deep coloured, soft red for blending and easy bottles.

wines.note: Dry Pinot Noir of medium body, red cherry, smoke and a slate edge, often raised in barrique; serve a touch below room temperature with duck, lamb, mushrooms or game birds.
From a classified site such as Walporzheimer Kräuterberg or Dernauer Pfarrwingert: denser, structured, oak aged Pinot built for a decade; decant a young vintage.
Softer, darker and rounder than Spätburgunder, with plum and violet; drink it younger, with roast pork or a veal chop.
A white wine pressed gently from Pinot Noir before the skins give colour: pale, dry and crisp, an aperitif and a partner for river fish.
A rosé from one red grape, Spätburgunder or Portugieser, off dry in the old style and dry today; a summer glass.
A small crop on slate, dry or feinherb, lime and wet stone, lighter than the valley's reds suggest.

made.viticulture: The upper valley is terraced and walled, worked by hand on slopes that no tractor can climb; the lower valley is gentler and partly mechanised. The old high yielding German Pinot clones have given way to tighter Burgundian selections, planted densely, pruned short and green harvested so that the small crop ripens its skins as well as its sugar. Picking runs from late September into October, later than the loess sites would need, because the growers wait for phenolic ripeness. Frost in the valley floor, a wet harvest and the labour of the walls are the constant hazards. The cooperative at Mayschoss, founded in 1868 and the oldest in Germany, still farms a large share of the valley beside the private estates. A red wine hiking trail, the Rotweinwanderweg, runs the length of the vineyards, and the tourism it carries has always paid for the terraces.
made.winemaking: The modern Ahr makes Pinot Noir the Burgundian way: grapes destemmed or partly left whole, a cold soak, fermentation in open vats with punching down, malolactic in barrel and twelve to eighteen months in French oak, a share of it new for the top sites, then bottling with little fining or filtration. The wines are dry. The older style, a pale, sweetish red stopped with sugar or back sweetened for the coach parties, survives at the cheaper end but no longer sets the tone. Blanc de Noir is pressed at once and fermented cool like a white; Weissherbst takes a few hours on the skins. Frühburgunder is handled the same way as Spätburgunder but drinks sooner. A little Sekt is made from Pinot by the traditional method.

law.classification: The Ahr follows the national ladder: Qualitätswein from the region, Prädikatswein above it, the dryness words beside it. It has a single Bereich, Walporzheim/Ahrtal, a single Grosslage, Klosterberg, and around forty Einzellagen, so a vineyard name on an Ahr label is almost always a true single site. The VDP's Ahr members classify their best slopes as Grosse Lage and make dry Spätburgunder Grosses Gewächs from them, held back a year longer than a white GG before release. Under the 2021 federal law the Grosslage will be labelled as a Region and Grosses Gewächs becomes a legal term for the valley's dry single vineyard reds.

A rosé of one red grape, Qualitätswein or above.

places.name: Altenahr
places.note: The upper end of the vineyards, where the valley is a rock gorge: the Eck, slate and greywacke, late ripening and tense.

places.name: Mayschoss
places.note: Home of the cooperative founded in 1868, the oldest in Germany; the Mönchberg on steep slate above the village.

places.name: Rech
places.note: A small village on a tight bend; the Herrenberg, slate and greywacke, makes firm, long lived Spätburgunder.

places.name: Dernau
places.note: The upper valley's leading village: the Pfarrwingert, a terraced slate bowl, and the Hardtberg above it; the dry Burgundian turn of the 1980s began here.

places.name: Marienthal
places.note: A former convent and later the state domaine of the Ahr; the Klostergarten and Trotzenberg on slate below the ruin.

places.name: Walporzheim
places.note: The Kräuterberg, a steep south facing wall of slate, and the Gärkammer, one of the smallest single vineyards in Germany; the valley's grandest Pinot Noir and the Bereich's name.

places.name: Ahrweiler
places.note: The walled medieval town where the valley opens: the Rosenthal and Silberberg on loess and loam over slate give rounder, riper, earlier Spätburgunder.

places.name: Bad Neuenahr
places.note: The spa town beside Ahrweiler; the Sonnenberg, a broad slope of loess and slate, ripe and generous.

places.name: Heimersheim
places.note: The last village before the Rhine plain, on loess: the Landskrone and Burggarten, the warmest, softest wines of the valley.

producers.name: Meyer-Näkel

producers.name: Jean Stodden
producers.why: Rech; small, firmly structured Spätburgunder from the Herrenberg, long aged in oak.

producers.name: Deutzerhof
producers.why: Mayschoss; dense, ripe Spätburgunder from the upper valley's slate, among the first to prove the valley could make serious red.

producers.name: J.J. Adeneuer
producers.why: Ahrweiler; holder of the tiny Gärkammer monopole and classic Walporzheim and Ahrweiler sites.

producers.name: Kreuzberg
producers.why: Dernau; polished, modern Pinot Noir from Pfarrwingert and Hardtberg.

producers.name: Winzergenossenschaft Mayschoss-Altenahr
producers.why: The cooperative of 1868, the oldest in Germany, still a large share of the valley and a fair glass of its red.

producers.name: Nelles
producers.why: Heimersheim; an old family house of the lower valley making dry Spätburgunder and Frühburgunder on loess.

exam: Place the Ahr: a Rhine tributary south of Bonn, one of the most northerly red wine regions anywhere, and one of the smallest.
Name its grape and its speciality: Spätburgunder, with Frühburgunder as the early ripening cousin.
Say why Pinot Noir ripens here: the slate gorge, south facing walls, the Eifel's rain shadow.
Know the dry, oak aged style that replaced the sweet reds, and the houses that made the turn.
Carry three villages and a site each for the Advanced sitting: Walporzheimer Kräuterberg, Dernauer Pfarrwingert, Ahrweiler Rosenthal.
traps: The Ahr is not on the Mosel and not a white wine region: it is a Rhine tributary and grows red.
Frühburgunder is not an early picked Spätburgunder; it is a distinct early ripening mutation of Pinot Noir.
Blanc de Noir is a white wine, not a rosé; Weissherbst is the rosé, and only from one red grape.
Ahr Spätburgunder is dry today; the old sweetish red was a tourist style, not the rule.
Sites read village then vineyard: Walporzheimer Kräuterberg, the village with its -er ending first.

cards.b: Germany's red wine valley: Spätburgunder on steep slate and greywacke in a sheltered gorge south of Bonn, dry and barrel aged since the 1980s.
Spätburgunder (lead, about two thirds), Frühburgunder (early Pinot mutation, the speciality), Portugieser, a little Riesling.
Upper: Altenahr to Dernau, slate and greywacke, steep, mineral and tense. Lower: Ahrweiler to Heimersheim, loess and loam, rounder, earlier.
Walporzheimer Kräuterberg and Gärkammer, Dernauer Pfarrwingert and Hardtberg, Ahrweiler Rosenthal and Silberberg, Neuenahrer Sonnenberg, Recher Herrenberg, Mayschosser Mönchberg.
One Bereich, Walporzheim/Ahrtal; one Grosslage, Klosterberg; around forty Einzellagen, so a vineyard name is nearly always a true single site.

cards.f: The Ahr's history in three dates
cards.b: 1868 the Mayschoss cooperative, Germany's oldest; the 1980s the dry Burgundian turn led at Dernau; July 2021 the flood that the valley has rebuilt from.

cards.f: Blanc de Noir on an Ahr list
cards.b: White wine from Spätburgunder pressed before the skins give colour: dry, pale, crisp; serve it as an aperitif or with river fish.

questions.q: Which grape covers the greatest share of the Ahr's vineyard?
questions.exp: Spätburgunder, Pinot Noir, fills about two thirds of the Ahr; Portugieser and Riesling are small shares and Dornfelder smaller still.

questions.q: Frühburgunder is an early ripening mutation of which grape?
questions.exp: Frühburgunder, Pinot Noir Précoce, ripens two to three weeks before Spätburgunder and gives softer, darker wine; the Ahr is its stronghold.

questions.q: Into which river does the Ahr flow?
questions.exp: The Ahr runs east out of the Eifel and joins the Rhine between Remagen and Sinzig, south of Bonn; it has nothing to do with the Mosel.

questions.q: Which rock makes the upper Ahr's steep vineyards so warm?
questions.exp: Dark Devonian slate with greywacke stores the day's sun and radiates it at night, and drains fast, which is why Pinot Noir ripens this far north.

questions.q: Which village holds the Gärkammer, one of Germany's smallest single vineyards?
questions.exp: The Gärkammer sits in Walporzheim beside the Kräuterberg; Dernau has the Pfarrwingert, Ahrweiler the Rosenthal and Mayschoss the Mönchberg.

questions.q: What does Blanc de Noir on an Ahr label describe?
opts: a white wine from red grapes, pressed before colour
a rosé from a single red grape
a pink wine from red and white grapes fermented together
a sparkling wine from Pinot Noir by the traditional method
questions.exp: Blanc de Noir is a white wine from red grapes, pressed at once so the skins give no colour; the rosé of one red grape is Weissherbst, the red and white co-ferment is Rotling and the sparkling wine is Sekt.

questions.q: What is the single Bereich of the Ahr called?
questions.exp: The whole valley is one Bereich, Walporzheim/Ahrtal, with one Grosslage, Klosterberg; the 2021 law will label the Grosslage as a Region.

regions.name: Mosel
regions.summary: The Mosel is the lightest great white wine on earth: Riesling on Devonian slate, on slopes so steep they are worked by hand, in a cool valley at the northern edge of ripeness. The river winds from Luxembourg through Trier and the Mittelmosel to Koblenz, and its two tributaries at Trier, the Saar and the Ruwer, carry the region's coolest, most austere wines. Kabinett at eight per cent with sugar and acid in balance, Spätlese and Auslese from sun and botrytis, Eiswein from frost and a growing dry school under the VDP's Grosses Gewächs all come from the same slate. Until 2007 the label said Mosel-Saar-Ruwer. Say MOH-zul.

terroir.climate: Cool continental, around 49 to 50 degrees north, with Atlantic cloud, moderate summers and long autumns. The slate stores the day's sun and gives it back after dark, the river bounces light into the slope and the valley walls keep off the wind, which together lift the vines over the ripening line. The Saar and Ruwer sit higher and colder, so their Riesling is picked later and keeps more acid.
terroir.soils: Devonian slate, blue grey through most of the Mittelmosel and the Saar, weathered to a thin, free draining topsoil that forces roots deep and warms quickly. At Ürzig and Erden the slate turns red with iron and volcanic rhyolite, giving spicier wines; the Ruwer is slate with more loam, the Terrassenmosel slate and quartzite, and the Obermosel above Trier is Muschelkalk limestone and Keuper marl.
terroir.topography: A deeply cut, meandering valley; the vineyards face south and south west on the outside of each bend, the inside bends being flat. Gradients run from 30 degrees to the 65 degrees of the Bremmer Calmont, counted the steepest vineyard in Europe. The Saar is wider and more open, the Ruwer a small side valley; altitude is low, so slope and aspect decide the site.
terroir.water: The Mosel, some 545 kilometres from the Vosges to the Rhine at Koblenz, reflects light and holds warmth; the Saar joins above Trier from the south, the Ruwer just below it from the east. Mists feed botrytis in autumn and frost settles on the valley floor.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.styles: About three fifths of the vineyard and all of its fame: Kabinett at 7.5 to 9 per cent with natural sweetness, Spätlese and Auslese from botrytis, Eiswein, and a dry school of stony, lime scented wines at 11 to 13 per cent.

grapes.name: Müller-Thurgau
grapes.styles: The second grape by area, on flat land and in the Obermosel: soft, floral, early drinking and much of it anonymous.

grapes.name: Elbling
grapes.styles: The Roman grape of the Obermosel's limestone: pale, tart, low in alcohol, a still wine for the local table and a Sekt base.

grapes.name: Pinot Blanc
grapes.styles: Weissburgunder on the limestone of the upper river and the gentler slopes: dry, round, a food white.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: A small, growing crop of dry Spätburgunder on the warmer bends and the Terrassenmosel, light and cherried.

wines.note: Seven and a half to nine per cent, green apple, lime and wet slate, sugar and acid in a balance that reads nearly dry; well chilled, with Thai or Vietnamese dishes, crab or trout.
Riper and fuller, peach and apricot over the slate, eight to nine per cent when sweet or eleven to twelve when trocken; the sweet version with pork and fruit.
Selected bunches touched by botrytis: honey, dried apricot and a nervy acid line. A gold capsule marks a richer selection, a long gold capsule richer still; with fruit tarts or blue cheese.

wines.style: Mosel Riesling trocken and Grosses Gewächs
wines.note: The dry Mosel: eleven to thirteen per cent, austere, stony, lime and herb; a GG comes from a Grosse Lage such as Wehlener Sonnenuhr. With fish, pork and roast chicken.
Off dry without a legal number, the valley's house style: a few grams of sweetness rounding the acid; the most versatile glass with spiced food.
BA and TBA from shrivelled botrytised berries in tiny volumes; Eiswein from healthy fruit frozen on the vine, pure and piercing. Half bottles, a dessert of their own.
Riesling or Elbling base wine, lean and high in acid, often a Winzersekt by the traditional method; an aperitif.

made.viticulture: The Mosel vine stands alone on a single pole, the Einzelpfahl, its two canes bent into a heart and tied to the stake with no wires. Many old plots on slate are ungrafted, phylloxera being ill at home in the dry, stony ground, and vines of a century are not rare. The slopes are too steep for tractors: the work is by hand, with winches and monorack rails on the worst walls. Harvest runs from early October into November in several passes, the selective picking that gives Spätlese and Auslese their names, and an Eiswein crop waits on the vine into December or January. Erosion, spring frost, hail and botrytis coming too early or not at all are the hazards.
made.winemaking: Whole bunches are pressed gently, the must settled and fermented cool in stainless steel or in the Fuder, the Mosel's thousand litre cask of old, neutral oak. The traditional houses let wild yeasts work and stop the fermentation by chilling and racking, leaving natural grape sugar behind at eight or nine per cent alcohol. The wines rest on their lees over winter and are bottled in spring, each lot with its own AP number. The dry school ferments through to eleven to thirteen per cent and holds its Grosses Gewächs under 9 grams of sugar. No new oak, no malolactic: the slate is the flavour. The richest Auslesen go to the September auctions: the VDP's Grosser Ring sells at Trier, and the Bernkasteler Ring, founded in 1899, holds its own on the Mittelmosel.

law.classification: The national ladder applies, and the Mosel's minimum must weights are the lowest in Germany: for Riesling, Kabinett at 70 degrees Oechsle, Spätlese 76, Auslese 83, Beerenauslese and Eiswein 110, Trockenbeerenauslese 150. The region was Mosel-Saar-Ruwer until 2007. It has six Bereiche: Burg Cochem for the lower terraces, Bernkastel for the Mittelmosel, Obermosel and Moseltor for the limestone upriver, Saar and Ruwertal. Its Grosslagen, Piesporter Michelsberg, Zeller Schwarze Katz, Kröver Nacktarsch and Wiltinger Scharzberg among them, carry the word Region from the 2026 vintage under the 2021 law. The VDP's Grosser Ring classifies the great sites as Grosse Lage; the dry wine from one is a Grosses Gewächs, always Riesling here, and the sweet wines keep their Prädikat.
tiers: Qualitätswein Mosel
Quality wine from anywhere in the region; may be chaptalised; the base of most trocken and feinherb bottles.
Kabinett
At least 70 degrees Oechsle for Riesling, the lightest floor in Germany; classically 7.5 to 9 per cent with natural sweetness.
Spätlese
At least 76 degrees: late picked, riper, peach over slate; sweet or trocken.
Auslese
At least 83 degrees: selected bunches, botrytis welcome; Goldkapsel for the richer lots.
Beerenauslese and Eiswein
At least 110 degrees: BA from botrytised berries, Eiswein from healthy grapes frozen on the vine at minus 7 °C or colder.
Trockenbeerenauslese
At least 150 degrees: shrivelled botrytised berries, a few hundred bottles from a great site.
VDP.Grosse Lage / Grosses Gewächs
A classified site such as the Doctor, the Sonnenuhr or the Scharzhofberg; its dry Riesling is the GG, released from 1 September of the year after harvest.
labels: The region's legal name until 2007; an old bottle, not another region.
A gold capsule on an Auslese for a richer, more botrytised selection; Lange Goldkapsel richer again, often an auction lot.
Old vines, on the Mosel often ungrafted on slate.
The Mosel's thousand litre cask of old oak.
Off dry, a trade word with no legal sugar limit; the valley's everyday style.
A district blend from anywhere on the Mittelmosel, not a wine of Bernkastel.
A vineyard estate with village standing, labelled without a village name: Scharzhofberger, Maximin Grünhäuser.

places.name: Mittelmosel (Bereich Bernkastel)
places.note: The heart of the region, from Trier downstream to Zell, holding nearly every famous site on blue slate at the outside bends of Piesport, Brauneberg, Bernkastel, Graach, Wehlen, Ürzig and Erden.

places.name: Trittenheim
places.note: Upstream of Piesport, the Apotheke on a sharp bend: delicate, floral Riesling.

places.name: Piesport
places.note: A horseshoe bend of slate facing due south: Goldtröpfchen, the little drop of gold, gives ripe, peachy, honeyed Riesling. The Grosslage Piesporter Michelsberg borrows the name for flat land across the river.

places.name: Brauneberg
places.note: The Juffer and the Juffer-Sonnenuhr, a south facing slate wall across the river from the village: rich, rounded, counted the Mosel's grandest in Napoleon's day.

places.name: Bernkastel
places.note: The tourist town beneath the Doctor, a tiny, near vertical grey slate site named for the archbishop it supposedly cured in 1360: smoky, dense, long lived.

places.name: Graach
places.note: Between Bernkastel and Wehlen: Himmelreich, broad and reliable, and Domprobst, steeper and deeper with more loam; firmer wines than Wehlen's.

places.name: Wehlen
places.note: The Sonnenuhr, a sundial set in the slate wall across the river, is the Mosel's most elegant site: floral, weightless, creamy with age.

places.name: Zeltingen
places.note: Next to Wehlen with its own Sonnenuhr and the Schlossberg: fuller and broader.

places.name: Ürzig
places.note: The Würzgarten, the spice garden, on red volcanic slate beneath the cliffs: the most exotic Mosel Riesling, spicy, tropical, firm.

places.name: Erden
places.note: Across the river from Ürzig: the Treppchen, the little stairs, on classic slate, and the Prälat, a tiny red slate amphitheatre between rock and river, counted the warmest site of the Mittelmosel.

places.name: Pünderich
places.note: The Marienburg, a long slate amphitheatre across from the village, at the lower end of the Mittelmosel where the terraces begin: dry GG and sweet wines both.

places.name: Saar
places.note: The Saar joins the Mosel above Trier from the south: a wider, colder valley where Riesling ripens last and keeps the most acid. Wiltingen's Scharzhofberg is its grand cru.

places.name: Wiltingen
places.note: The Scharzhofberg is an Ortsteil, so the label reads Scharzhofberger without the village: grey slate on a south facing hill, among the most sought after Riesling vineyards in Germany. The Grosslage Wiltinger Scharzberg is a different thing.

places.name: Ockfen
places.note: The Bockstein, a south facing slate bowl: the classic Saar Kabinett and Spätlese site after the Scharzhofberg.

places.name: Kanzem
places.note: The Altenberg, red slate on a steep bend and among the Saar's warmest sites.

places.name: Ayl
places.note: The Kupp, a long slate slope in many parcels: precise, lime scented Riesling, often dry.

places.name: Saarburg
places.note: The Rausch, diabase and slate above the town, famous for Eiswein and Auslese.

places.name: Ruwer
places.note: A small stream joining the Mosel just below Trier from the east; the vineyards sit in a side valley on slate with loam and give Riesling of great delicacy, herbs and blackcurrant leaf.

places.name: Mertesdorf and Maximin Grünhaus
places.note: A former Benedictine estate's three walled sites, Abtsberg, Herrenberg and Bruderberg, the abbot's, the lords' and the brothers', in that order of rank; labelled Maximin Grünhäuser.

places.name: Eitelsbach
places.note: The Karthäuserhofberg, once Carthusian, known for the small neck label its bottles wear.

places.name: Terrassenmosel (Bereich Burg Cochem)
places.note: From Zell down to Koblenz the valley narrows into a gorge of terraces held by dry stone walls. It is slightly warmer, the slate harder and mixed with quartzite, the wines firmer and more savoury: the Mosel's dry stronghold.

places.name: Zell
places.note: The town of the Grosslage Zeller Schwarze Katz, the black cat, a label the world drank by the million; its own single sites are better than the name.

places.name: Alf
places.note: A small village between Zell and Cochem at the mouth of a side valley, with steep terraced parcels of its own and, at neighbouring Sankt Aldegund, the Palmberg terraces, where old vines survive.

places.name: Bremm
places.note: The Calmont, at up to 65 degrees counted the steepest vineyard in Europe, worked by monorack rail.

places.name: Winningen
places.note: Near Koblenz: the Uhlen, bottled by its sub-soils, and the Röttgen on hard slate terraces; the lower Mosel's greatest dry Rieslings.

places.name: Obermosel and Moseltor
places.note: Upstream of Trier the Mosel is the border with Luxembourg and the rock changes to Muschelkalk limestone and Keuper marl: Elbling, the Roman grape, makes light, tart still wine and Sekt here, with Pinot Blanc and Pinot Gris rising.

producers.name: Egon Müller
producers.why: The Scharzhof at Wiltingen; its Scharzhofberger from Kabinett to TBA sets the price of Saar Riesling at the Trier auctions.

producers.name: Joh. Jos. Prüm
producers.why: Wehlen, founded 1911; Wehlener Sonnenuhr Kabinett to Auslese, famously slow to open, never dry.

producers.name: Fritz Haag
producers.why: Brauneberg; the Juffer-Sonnenuhr in every Prädikat, the model of Mittelmosel balance.

producers.name: Dr. Loosen
producers.why: Bernkastel; old ungrafted vines in Ürzig, Erden, Wehlen and Graach, the house that carried Mosel Riesling onto the world's lists.

producers.name: Willi Schaefer
producers.why: Graach; a tiny estate in Domprobst and Himmelreich, crystalline Kabinett and Spätlese.

producers.name: Markus Molitor
producers.why: Bernkastel-Wehlen; a large range coded by capsule colour, white for dry, green for feinherb, gold for sweet, across dozens of sites.

producers.name: Dr. Hermann
producers.why: Erden; Erdener Prälat and Treppchen and Ürziger Würzgarten from old ungrafted vines, Prädikat wines of purity.

producers.name: C.H. Berres
producers.why: Ürzig; an old family house in the Würzgarten and Erdener Treppchen, old vine Riesling at fair prices.

producers.name: Clemens Busch
producers.why: Pünderich; biodynamic dry Riesling from parcels of the Marienburg bottled by the colour of their slate.

producers.name: Weingut Stein
producers.why: Alf; terraced old vines on the lower Mosel, feinherb and dry, an independent voice.

producers.name: Van Volxem
producers.why: Wiltingen; the Saar's dry revival, Scharzhofberger and Gottesfuss picked at full ripeness.

producers.name: Forstmeister Geltz Zilliken
producers.why: Saarburg; the Rausch, long cask ageing in a deep cellar, celebrated Eiswein and Auslese.

producers.name: Peter Lauer
producers.why: Ayl; Kupp parcels numbered by cask, mostly dry and feinherb, and Saar Sekt.

producers.name: Wwe. Dr. H. Thanisch, Erben Thanisch
producers.why: Bernkastel; a principal owner of the Doctor since the nineteenth century.

producers.name: Maximin Grünhaus
producers.why: Mertesdorf on the Ruwer; Abtsberg, Herrenberg and Bruderberg in every style.

producers.name: Karthäuserhof
producers.why: Eitelsbach; the Ruwer's other great estate, the Karthäuserhofberg in every Prädikat.

producers.name: Reinhold Haart
producers.why: Piesport; the leading grower of the Goldtröpfchen.

producers.name: Heymann-Löwenstein
producers.why: Winningen; the Terrassenmosel's dry pioneer, Uhlen bottled by rock type.

producers.name: Selbach-Oster
producers.why: Zeltingen; Sonnenuhr and Schlossberg across the full Prädikat range.

exam: The Mosel against the Rheingau: lighter, lower in alcohol, slate, more often sweet; the Rheingau drier, fuller, with higher must weight floors.
The Saar and Ruwer: the coldest, highest acid Rieslings, and the name Mosel-Saar-Ruwer that ended in 2007.
Sites by village: Wehlener Sonnenuhr, Bernkasteler Doctor, Ürziger Würzgarten, Erdener Prälat, Brauneberger Juffer-Sonnenuhr, Piesporter Goldtröpfchen, Scharzhofberger.
The Grosslage traps: Piesporter Michelsberg, Zeller Schwarze Katz, Kröver Nacktarsch, Wiltinger Scharzberg.
Kabinett arithmetic: 70 degrees Oechsle minimum, 7.5 to 9 per cent alcohol, sugar read against acid.
The Goldkapsel and the Trier auctions: how a house marks its richest Auslese.
For Advanced and Master: the six Bereiche, the Terrassenmosel's dry school, the Obermosel's Elbling on limestone.
traps: Scharzhofberger is the single vineyard, an Ortsteil labelled without Wiltingen; Wiltinger Scharzberg is the Grosslage. One letter of difference, a world of price.
Piesporter Michelsberg is a Grosslage over flat land, not the Goldtröpfchen slope.
Mosel-Saar-Ruwer on a label is an old bottle, not a different region: the name became Mosel in 2007.
A Mosel Kabinett tastes sweet but is modest in sugar; its acid makes forty grams read like half that.
The Doctor is in Bernkastel, the Sonnenuhr in Wehlen and in Zeltingen, the Würzgarten in Ürzig: the village is the first word.
Bereich Bernkastel on a label is a district blend from anywhere on the Mittelmosel, not a Bernkastel wine.
Red slate at Ürzig and Erden is volcanic in origin; blue slate is the norm. Both are Devonian, both drain and warm.

cards.b: Riesling on Devonian slate, slopes to 65 degrees, a cool winding valley: the lightest great white wine, 7.5 to 9 per cent when sweet, austere and stony when dry.
Mosel (Mittelmosel: Bernkastel, Wehlen, Ürzig, Piesport); Saar (Wiltingen, Ockfen, Ayl, Saarburg: colder, higher acid); Ruwer (Maximin Grünhaus, Karthäuserhof: delicate). Mosel-Saar-Ruwer until 2007.
Kabinett 70, Spätlese 76, Auslese 83, BA and Eiswein 110, TBA 150 degrees Oechsle: the lowest Kabinett floor in Germany.

cards.f: The six Bereiche of the Mosel
cards.b: Burg Cochem (the terraces), Bernkastel (Mittelmosel), Obermosel, Moseltor, Saar, Ruwertal.
Piesporter Michelsberg, Zeller Schwarze Katz, Kröver Nacktarsch, Wiltinger Scharzberg, Bernkasteler Kurfürstlay. Badstube is the small, respectable exception.
Scharzhofberger, Wehlener Sonnenuhr, Bernkasteler Doctor, Graacher Domprobst, Ürziger Würzgarten, Erdener Prälat, Brauneberger Juffer-Sonnenuhr.
A gold capsule on an Auslese marks a richer, more botrytised selection within the Prädikat; Lange Goldkapsel richer again, often the auction lot.
The Mosel's traditional cask of about a thousand litres, old and neutral; the Rhine's Stück holds twelve hundred.
The lower Mosel from Zell to Koblenz: terraces on hard slate and quartzite, Winninger Uhlen and Röttgen, Bremmer Calmont; the dry Mosel's stronghold.

questions.q: On which tributary of the Mosel does Wiltingen stand?
questions.exp: Wiltingen and its Scharzhofberg are on the Saar, which joins the Mosel above Trier; the Ruwer is the smaller stream below Trier, and the Nahe and Lahn are Rhine tributaries.

questions.q: In which village does the Doctor vineyard lie?
questions.exp: The Bernkasteler Doctor is the tiny grey slate site above the town; Wehlen has the Sonnenuhr, Graach the Himmelreich and Domprobst, Piesport the Goldtröpfchen.

questions.q: In which year was the region’s name shortened from Mosel-Saar-Ruwer to Mosel?
questions.exp: The region was Mosel-Saar-Ruwer until 2007, when the name became simply Mosel; an old bottle carrying the long name is the same region, not a different one.

questions.q: What is the minimum must weight for a Mosel Riesling Kabinett?
questions.exp: The Mosel's floors are the lowest in Germany: Kabinett 70, Spätlese 76, Auslese 83, Beerenauslese and Eiswein 110 degrees Oechsle; the Rheingau asks 73 for Kabinett.

questions.q: Which grape grows on the Obermosel's limestone, where Riesling gives way?
questions.exp: Upstream of Trier the slate ends and Muschelkalk limestone begins; Elbling, the Roman grape, makes light, tart still wine and Sekt base there.

questions.q: Which of these Mosel names is a single vineyard rather than a Grosslage?
questions.exp: The Treppchen is a registered Einzellage at Erden; the black cat of Zell, the bare bottom of Kröv and the Michelsberg of Piesport are collective Grosslage names.

questions.q: Which rock underlies the Ürziger Würzgarten and gives it its spicy character?
questions.exp: Ürzig and the Erdener Prälat sit on red slate coloured by iron and volcanic rhyolite; blue slate is the Mittelmosel norm and the limestone and marl belong to the Obermosel.

questions.q: What alcohol does a classic sweet Mosel Riesling Kabinett carry?
questions.exp: Fermentation is stopped early to keep natural sugar, so a sweet Kabinett lands at 7.5 to 9 per cent; the dry school and the GG run at 11 to 13.

regions.name: Rheingau
regions.summary: The Rheingau is thirty kilometres of north bank where the Rhine, blocked by the Taunus, turns west between Wiesbaden and Rüdesheim, so the whole slope looks south across a broad stretch of water. It is the Riesling region of history: the Cistercians at Kloster Eberbach, Schloss Johannisberg's Spätlese legend of 1775, the Charta growers who put dry Riesling back on the table in 1984 and the Erstes Gewächs law of 1999. Riesling fills nearly four fifths of the vineyard; Spätburgunder owns Assmannshausen, where the river turns north into its gorge. The wines are fuller and firmer than the Mosel's, more often dry, with peach, quince and a smoky mineral grip. Hochheim, apart on the Main, gave English the word Hock.

terroir.climate: Cool continental tempered by the river and shielded by the Taunus, whose forested ridge stops the north wind; the south facing bank gathers sun all day and the Rhine, broad and slow here, reflects it back. Autumn mists off the water bring botrytis for Auslese and above, and the long season lets Riesling ripen fully while keeping its acid. Rainfall is moderate; the sites nearest the river are warmest, the ones up towards the forest coolest and latest.
terroir.soils: Varied along the slope: at Rüdesheim and Assmannshausen in the west, slate and Taunus quartzite on steep ground, which is why Pinot Noir and the fieriest Riesling live there; through the centre, from Geisenheim to Erbach, deep loess and loam over sandstone and marl, giving the broad, ripe style of Johannisberg and Marcobrunn; at Kiedrich and Rauenthal, phyllite and slate on higher ground, spicy and mineral; at Hochheim, Tertiary limestone and marl beside the Main.
terroir.topography: A long, gentle south facing slope rather than a gorge: the vines rise from the river terrace at about 80 metres to around 300 metres at the forest edge, steepest at the western end where the Rüdesheimer Berg drops to the river and the Rhine itself turns north through the Binger Loch into the Mittelrhein gorge past Assmannshausen and Lorch. The villages sit in a line along the foot of the slope; the best sites are mid-slope.
terroir.water: The Rhine, flowing east to west for the length of the region, moderating frost, storing warmth and lighting the slope; its width here matters more than anywhere else in Germany. The Main joins it at Mainz; Hochheim's vines, a few kilometres up the smaller river, face the Main rather than the Rhine. Mists off both feed botrytis.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.styles: Nearly four fifths of the vineyard: dry, firm, peach and quince with a smoky grip, from Charta and Erstes Gewächs to GG, and the botrytis Auslese, BA and TBA that the region named.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Spätburgunder, about one vine in eight, concentrated at Assmannshausen on the Höllenberg's slate: dry, oak aged, red cherry and earth.

grapes.name: Müller-Thurgau
grapes.styles: Bred at Geisenheim in 1882 and planted on the flatter ground: soft, floral, early.

grapes.name: Pinot Blanc
grapes.styles: Weissburgunder in small plots, dry and creamy, a food white beside the Riesling.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: A little, mostly for Sekt and a few oaked dry whites.

wines.note: The regional staple: dry, medium bodied, peach and quince with a smoky edge, 12 to 13 per cent; with pork schnitzel, roast chicken, river fish and asparagus.

Dry Riesling from a classified site such as Rüdesheimer Berg Schlossberg, Kiedricher Gräfenberg or Erbacher Marcobrunn: firm, long, built for ten years; decant it young and serve it with richer fish and veal.
Lightly sweet and fuller than the Mosel's at 9 to 11 per cent, apricot and honey over stone; a Spätlese with spiced pork or a fruit stuffed bird.
The botrytis tradition the Rheingau named: Spätlese and Auslese were coined at Johannisberg, and a TBA from Kiedrich or Rauenthal is among the longest lived sweet wines in the world.
Pinot Noir from the Höllenberg's slate: pale to medium ruby, red cherry, earth and smoke, dry and oak aged; with duck, lamb and game.
Riesling base wine from the cooler sites by the traditional method, lean and lively; an aperitif and the house pour at Eltville's sparkling cellars.
From the Main rather than the Rhine, on limestone and marl: rounder, earthier, the wine the English called Hock.

made.viticulture: The Rheingau trains Riesling on wires, one or two canes in the Guyot manner, and the gentler central slopes can be worked by tractor; only the slate walls of the Rüdesheimer Berg and Assmannshausen ask for the Mosel's hand labour. Land consolidation in the twentieth century terraced and reshaped much of the slope. Clonal selection is a local science: the research and teaching institute at Geisenheim, founded in 1872, bred Müller-Thurgau in 1882 and supplies the Riesling clones most of Germany plants. Harvest runs from late September into November, with selective passes for the Prädikate and a watch on the river mists that bring botrytis; frost at the forest edge, hail and downy mildew in a wet summer are the hazards. The Spätlese legend of 1775 belongs here: the courier bringing the abbot's permission to pick at Johannisberg arrived late, the grapes had rotted on the vine, and the wine was the best anyone had made. Yields for Erstes Gewächs and GG are capped well below the regional norm.
made.winemaking: The Rhine's cask is the Stück, twelve hundred litres of old oak, though stainless steel now does most of the fermenting. The region's modern identity is dry: the Charta growers of 1984 set a standard for trocken and halbtrocken Riesling picked at higher must weight, and the Erstes Gewächs rules that followed in 1999 asked for classified sites, dry wine and a tasting panel. Fermentation runs to the end at 12 to 13 per cent, malolactic is avoided to keep the acid line, and the wines rest on their lees into spring; a GG waits until 1 September of the year after harvest. The sweet tradition continues from Kabinett to TBA by stopping the ferment or by botrytis concentration, with Eiswein in the cold years. Assmannshausen's Pinot Noir is fermented in open vats and aged in barrique, a style the state domaine kept alive when no one else in Germany made serious red. Eltville houses several sparkling wine cellars working the traditional method on Riesling.

law.classification: The Rheingau is a single Bereich, Johannisberg, with a handful of Grosslagen such as Johannisberger Erntebringer and Rüdesheimer Burgweg, and its minimum must weights sit above the Mosel's: for Riesling, Kabinett 73 degrees Oechsle, Spätlese 85, Auslese 95, Beerenauslese and Eiswein 125, Trockenbeerenauslese 150. Four estates hold Ortsteil status and are labelled without a village: Schloss Johannisberg, Schloss Vollrads, Steinberg and Schloss Reichartshausen. The region wrote its own first growth law: the Charta association of 1984 led to the state of Hesse recognising Erstes Gewächs in 1999 for dry Riesling and Spätburgunder from classified sites, the only such legal term in Germany for two decades. The VDP's Rheingau members moved to Grosses Gewächs from the 2012 vintage, and the federal law of 2021 makes both Erstes Gewächs and Grosses Gewächs national terms for dry single vineyard wine.
tiers: Qualitätswein Rheingau
Quality wine from the region; may be chaptalised; the dry everyday bottle.
Kabinett to Trockenbeerenauslese
Rheingau floors for Riesling: 73, 85, 95, 125, 125 and 150 degrees Oechsle, higher than the Mosel's at every step.
Charta
The growers' standard of 1984: Riesling only, dry or halbtrocken, picked riper than the law asks, from Rheingau sites, the double Romanesque arch on the bottle.
Erstes Gewächs
The Rheingau's legal first growth from 1999: dry Riesling or Spätburgunder from classified sites, tasted by a panel; now a national term under the 2021 law.
VDP.Grosse Lage / Grosses Gewächs
The VDP's top site and its dry wine, used by Rheingau members since the 2012 vintage in place of Erstes Gewächs.
labels: The old English word for Rhine wine, from Hochheim.
A castle estate; Schloss Johannisberg and Schloss Vollrads are Ortsteile labelled without a village name.
Wine of the Steinberg, Kloster Eberbach's walled vineyard, an Ortsteil of Hattenheim.
The Rhine's twelve hundred litre cask.
The whole Rheingau as one district; a district blend, not a Johannisberg wine.

places.name: Lorch
places.note: Beyond the bend, in the Mittelrhein gorge but legally Rheingau: slate, steep, Riesling late and lean; Bodental-Steinberg and Krone.

places.name: Assmannshausen
places.note: Where the river turns north: the Höllenberg, slate and phyllite, the home of Rheingau Spätburgunder for centuries and the state domaine's red cellar.

places.name: Rüdesheim
places.note: The Rüdesheimer Berg, the steep western end on slate and quartzite above the river: Berg Schlossberg, the finest and driest, Berg Roseneck and Berg Rottland; Bischofsberg, Drachenstein and Klosterlay on gentler ground. Ripe even in cool years.

places.name: Geisenheim
places.note: Rothenberg and Kläuserweg on loess tinged with slate, and the research and teaching institute of 1872 where Müller-Thurgau was bred; Johannisberg is one of its districts.

places.name: Johannisberg
places.note: Schloss Johannisberg above the village, Benedictine from about 1100, planted to Riesling alone from 1720 and the birthplace of the Spätlese in 1775; the castle is an Ortsteil. Hölle and Klaus lie beside it.

places.name: Winkel
places.note: Jesuitengarten and Hasensprung on loess and loam: ripe, generous Riesling; Schloss Vollrads above the village, selling wine since 1211, is an Ortsteil.

places.name: Oestrich
places.note: Lenchen and Doosberg, broad sites near the river with the old wine crane on the bank: ripe, fruity Riesling and fine Auslese.

places.name: Hallgarten
places.note: The highest village, cool, late and firm: Schönhell and Jungfer give Riesling with acid and length.

places.name: Hattenheim
places.note: Wisselbrunnen, Nussbrunnen and Mannberg on marl near the river, and above the village Kloster Eberbach, the Cistercian abbey of 1136, whose walled Steinberg is an Ortsteil labelled Steinberger. The Marcobrunn spring marks the border with Erbach.

places.name: Erbach
places.note: Marcobrunn, the brook of the border, on marl and loess by the river, long held the Rheingau's richest, most honeyed Riesling; Siegelsberg and Schlossberg beside it.

places.name: Kiedrich
places.note: Set back from the river on phyllite and slate: the Gräfenberg, spicy and racy, among the finest Riesling and TBA sites in Germany; Turmberg and Wasseros beside it.

places.name: Rauenthal
places.note: High above Eltville, late ripening and spicy: Baiken, Gehrn, Rothenberg and Nonnenberg give Rieslings that need years.

places.name: Eltville
places.note: The largest wine town, with the cellars of the Hessian state domaine and the sparkling houses; Sonnenberg and Langenstück on the slope.

places.name: Walluf
places.note: The eastern village before Wiesbaden; the Walkenberg and old Riesling parcels.

places.name: Hochheim
places.note: Apart on the Main east of Wiesbaden, on limestone and marl: Domdechaney, Kirchenstück, Hölle and Königin Victoriaberg, named for the queen's visit of 1845; rounder, earthier wines and the source of the word Hock.

producers.name: Schloss Johannisberg
producers.why: The Riesling monastery of 1720 and the Spätlese of 1775; its coloured capsules have coded the Prädikate since the nineteenth century.

producers.name: Schloss Vollrads
producers.why: Winkel; wine sold since 1211, a moated tower and dry Riesling in the Charta mould.

producers.name: Robert Weil
producers.why: Kiedrich; the Gräfenberg from dry GG to TBA, the Rheingau's reference for botrytis wine since the 1990s.

producers.name: Georg Breuer
producers.why: Rüdesheim; Berg Schlossberg and Nonnenberg, bone dry Riesling that led the Charta idea to its conclusion.

producers.name: Hessische Staatsweingüter Kloster Eberbach
producers.why: The state domaine at the abbey; Steinberg, Assmannshausen's Höllenberg reds and the abbey's medieval cellars.

producers.name: Künstler
producers.why: Hochheim; Domdechaney, Kirchenstück and Hölle, the proof that the Main's limestone makes grand dry Riesling.

producers.name: Leitz
producers.why: Rüdesheim; the Berg sites parcel by parcel, dry and sweet, widely poured by the glass.

producers.name: August Kesseler
producers.why: Assmannshausen; Höllenberg Spätburgunder that set the modern standard for Rheingau red.

producers.name: Peter Jakob Kühn
producers.why: Oestrich; biodynamic, long lees ageing, Doosberg and Lenchen with unusual depth.

exam: Geography first: the west running Rhine, the Taunus wall, the south facing bank; Hochheim on the Main, Assmannshausen at the gorge.
Style against the Mosel: fuller, drier, firmer, higher must weight floors, more Spätburgunder.
The dates the exam likes: Eberbach 1136, Johannisberg's Spätlese 1775, Charta 1984, Erstes Gewächs 1999.
Villages west to east with a site each; Schloss Johannisberg, Schloss Vollrads and Steinberg as Ortsteile.
Hock and its origin; Geisenheim and Müller-Thurgau's birth in 1882.
For Advanced: the soil shift from slate to loess to phyllite along the slope, and Rauenthal's late ripening.
traps: Erstes Gewächs was the Rheingau's own legal first growth, not the VDP's Erste Lage: cousins, not twins.
Hochheim is on the Main, not the Rhine, and belongs to the Rheingau all the same.
Steinberg is a vineyard, not a village; Steinberger on a label is an Ortsteil of Hattenheim.
Marcobrunn sits on the border of Hattenheim and Erbach and is labelled Erbacher.
Assmannshausen is the red island of a Riesling region, on slate; do not put Rheingau Spätburgunder at Johannisberg.
A Rheingau Kabinett needs 73 degrees Oechsle, not the Mosel's 70: each region sets its own floor.

cards.b: Thirty kilometres of south facing north bank where the Rhine runs west; Riesling four fifths, firmer and drier than the Mosel; Spätburgunder at Assmannshausen; Hochheim apart on the Main.
Kabinett 73, Spätlese 85, Auslese 95, BA and Eiswein 125, TBA 150 degrees Oechsle: higher floors than the Mosel's at every step.
1136 Kloster Eberbach founded; 1720 Riesling alone at Johannisberg; 1775 the Spätlese; 1872 Geisenheim; 1984 Charta; 1999 Erstes Gewächs in law; 2012 VDP members move to GG.
Lorch, Assmannshausen, Rüdesheim, Geisenheim, Johannisberg, Winkel, Oestrich, Hallgarten, Hattenheim, Erbach, Kiedrich, Rauenthal, Eltville, Walluf; Hochheim apart on the Main.

Rüdesheimer Berg Schlossberg, Schloss Johannisberg, Winkeler Jesuitengarten, Hattenheimer Wisselbrunnen, Steinberg, Erbacher Marcobrunn, Kiedricher Gräfenberg, Rauenthaler Baiken, Hochheimer Domdechaney, Assmannshäuser Höllenberg.
A growers' association of 1984 for dry and halbtrocken Riesling from Rheingau sites at higher ripeness, marked by a double Romanesque arch; the seed of Erstes Gewächs.
Schloss Johannisberg, Schloss Vollrads, Steinberg and Schloss Reichartshausen: estates with village standing, labelled without a village name.

cards.f: Hock: the word and its origin
cards.b: The English word for Rhine wine, from Hochheim; Queen Victoria's visit of 1845 gave the Königin Victoriaberg its name.

questions.q: Which hills shelter the Rheingau from the north?
questions.exp: The Taunus ridge turns the Rhine west and blocks the north wind; the Hunsrück shelters the Nahe, the Eifel the Ahr and the Haardt the Pfalz.

questions.q: Which estate claims the first Spätlese, from a late harvest in 1775?
questions.exp: The courier with the abbot's permission to pick arrived late at Johannisberg in 1775; the rotted grapes made a famous wine and gave the Spätlese its name.

questions.q: Which Rheingau village is known for Spätburgunder rather than Riesling?
questions.exp: Assmannshausen’s Höllenberg, on slate where the river turns north, has grown Pinot Noir for centuries; Rüdesheim, Hattenheim and Geisenheim are Riesling villages.

questions.q: On which river does Hochheim stand?
questions.exp: Hochheim lies on the Main just before it meets the Rhine at Mainz, apart from the rest of the Rheingau and on limestone rather than slate or loess.

questions.q: Which English word for Rhine wine comes from the name of Hochheim?
questions.exp: English merchants shortened Hochheimer to Hock and used it for any Rhine wine; Queen Victoria's 1845 visit fixed the association.

questions.q: In which year did Hesse recognise Erstes Gewächs as a legal term for the Rheingau?
questions.exp: Erstes Gewächs entered Hessian law in 1999 after the Charta growers' campaign; 1984 is Charta's founding and 2002 the VDP's first Grosses Gewächs elsewhere.

questions.q: Which site is the walled vineyard of Kloster Eberbach?
questions.exp: The Steinberg is the Cistercians' walled vineyard above Hattenheim, an Ortsteil labelled Steinberger; Marcobrunn is Erbach's, Gräfenberg Kiedrich's and Höllenberg Assmannshausen's.

questions.q: In which village is the Gräfenberg vineyard?
questions.exp: The Kiedricher Gräfenberg sits on phyllite and slate set back from the river, a source of dry GG and of some of Germany's finest TBA.

regions.name: Nahe
regions.summary: The Nahe flows north east out of the hills beyond Idar-Oberstein to the Rhine at Bingen, and its valley, between the Mosel and the Rheingau on the map and in the glass, is a small region of broken geology: slate, quartzite, volcanic porphyry, sandstone and loess within a few kilometres. Riesling is a little under a third of the vineyard and all of its fame, carrying the Mosel's delicacy with a little more flesh and a mineral, blackcurrant leaf tang. The middle valley from Schlossböckelheim to Bad Kreuznach holds the great names, Kupfergrube, Hermannshöhle and Brücke; the upper valley at Monzingen and the lower valley towards Bingen complete it. Say NAH-uh.

terroir.climate: Mild and dry, sheltered by the Hunsrück and its Soonwald ridge to the north and west, with a long, sunny autumn; rainfall is low, around 500 millimetres, and spring frost on the valley floor is the main hazard. The upper valley is cooler and later, the lower valley near Bingen warmer; Riesling ripens between Mosel and Rheingau dates.
terroir.soils: The most varied in Germany: Devonian slate and quartzite in the upper valley at Monzingen; volcanic porphyry and melaphyre around Schlossböckelheim, Niederhausen and Traisen; red sandstone, conglomerate and loess around Bad Kreuznach; loess, loam and gravel in the lower valley towards Bingen. Each gives a different Riesling, from the smoky, taut wines of the porphyry to the broader wines of the loam.
terroir.topography: A winding valley with steep, rocky south facing slopes on the outer bends and the Rotenfels, a red porphyry cliff above Traisen, as its landmark; side valleys such as Bockenau's hold cooler sites. Vineyards run from Martinstein in the upper valley some fifty kilometres to Bingen, and the single Bereich, Nahetal, covers all of it.
terroir.water: The Nahe, small and quick, with its tributaries the Glan, the Alsenz, the Ellerbach and the Gräfenbach; it moderates the air and lights the slopes. The Brücke vineyard sits on its bank at Oberhausen, catching the mists and frost that make Eiswein possible.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.styles: A little under a third of the vineyard: dry GG from porphyry and slate, lightly sweet Kabinett and Spätlese, botrytis Auslese and Eiswein, all with a smoky, blackcurrant leaf mineral line.

grapes.name: Müller-Thurgau
grapes.styles: Soft, floral white in volume on the loess and the flatter ground.

grapes.name: Dornfelder
grapes.styles: The valley's volume red: deep coloured, soft, plummy, dry or off dry.

grapes.name: Pinot Gris / Grigio
grapes.styles: Grauburgunder on loess and loam: round, nutty, dry, the everyday food white.

grapes.name: Pinot Blanc
grapes.styles: Weissburgunder, dry and creamy, often with a little oak.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: A small crop of dry Spätburgunder, light and cherried, mostly in the lower valley.

wines.note: Dry, medium bodied, grapefruit, blackcurrant leaf and wet stone at 12 to 13 per cent; with grilled fish, pork, chicken and vegetable dishes.
From Hermannshöhle, Kupfergrube, Felsenberg, Halenberg or Felseneck: smoky, taut and long; decant a young one, serve it with turbot or veal.
Lightly sweet at 8 to 10 per cent, apple, peach and herbs with the valley's mineral tang; a Spätlese with pork and apple or spiced dishes.
Botrytis Auslese with a gold capsule from the porphyry sites, and Eiswein from the Brücke's frost: honeyed, piercing, long lived.
Dry Pinot Blanc and Pinot Gris from the loess, round and nutty; the everyday white of the valley's inns.
A small crop of Pinot Noir, light, dry and cherried, served cool.

made.viticulture: Riesling takes the steep, rocky outer bends on porphyry and slate, where terraces and hand work are the rule and the thin soil keeps vigour low; the Pinots and Müller-Thurgau take the loess and loam that tractors can reach. Training is on wires, one or two canes. The dry climate means little rot pressure until the autumn mists arrive on purpose for Auslese, and the growers pick late into October and November, site by site, because each rock ripens at its own pace. Frost in the valley floor is the enemy and, at the Brücke, the friend: the vineyard lies low enough beside the river to freeze for Eiswein in many winters. The Prussian state domaine founded in 1902 at Niederhausen cleared the Kupfergrube from a former copper mine and the scrub above it over the following years, and the terraces it cut are still the middle valley's grandest. The valley was long sold as Rhine wine; it became an Anbaugebiet of its own only with the 1971 law.
made.winemaking: The Nahe cellar sits between its neighbours in method as in taste. Riesling is pressed whole bunch, settled and fermented cool in stainless steel or in old oak casks; the leading houses use wild yeasts and long lees contact for the dry wines, which ferment through to 12 to 13 per cent and are held under 9 grams of sugar for GG. The Prädikat wines are stopped by chilling to keep natural sweetness at 8 to 10 per cent, a little fuller than the Mosel's. Botrytis Auslese and Beerenauslese come from the porphyry sites in the misty years, and the Brücke's Eiswein is pressed frozen in the small hours. Gold capsules mark the richer Auslese lots as on the Mosel. The Pinots are fermented dry, some Weissburgunder with a share of barrel; Dornfelder is made soft and fruity. No new oak touches the Riesling: the rock is the point.

law.classification: The national ladder applies, and the Nahe is one Bereich, Nahetal, with a handful of Grosslagen whose names cause trouble: Rüdesheimer Rosengarten belongs to Rüdesheim an der Nahe and not to the Rheingau's Rüdesheim, Schlossböckelheimer Burgweg covers the middle valley around the true single sites Kupfergrube and Felsenberg, and Kreuznacher Kronenberg spreads over the town's hills. The Nahe was carved out as its own Anbaugebiet by the 1971 law after centuries of being sold as Rhine wine. The VDP's Nahe members classify the porphyry and slate sites as Grosse Lage and bottle dry Riesling Grosses Gewächs from them, with Kabinett, Spätlese, Auslese and Eiswein from the same slopes keeping their Prädikat. Under the 2021 federal law the Grosslagen take the word Region from the 2026 vintage and Grosses Gewächs becomes a legal term.
tiers: Qualitätswein Nahe
Quality wine from the region; may be chaptalised; the dry everyday bottle.
Prädikatswein
Kabinett to Trockenbeerenauslese by must weight; the floors match or sit a touch above the Mosel's, and Eiswein is a valley speciality.
VDP.Grosse Lage / Grosses Gewächs
Hermannshöhle, Kupfergrube, Felsenberg, Brücke, Bastei, Dellchen, Halenberg, Frühlingsplätzchen, Felseneck among the classified sites; the dry Riesling from one is the GG.
Nahetal
The single Bereich, from Martinstein to Bingen.
labels: A Nahe Grosslage from Rüdesheim an der Nahe, not the Rheingau's Rüdesheim.
A Grosslage over the middle valley; Kupfergrube and Felsenberg are the single sites.
As on the Mosel, a house's richer Auslese selection.
The Prussian state domaine of 1902 at Niederhausen that cleared the Kupfergrube; the estate continues under the name Gut Hermannsberg.

places.name: Upper Nahe
places.note: The cooler, later western end from Martinstein to Meddersheim, on slate, quartzite and sandstone: taut, lime scented Riesling that ages slowly.

places.name: Monzingen
places.note: Two classified sites face each other: the Halenberg, blue slate and quartzite, taut and smoky, and the Frühlingsplätzchen, red slate, fuller and more floral.

places.name: Meddersheim
places.note: The Rheingrafenberg, a south facing slope above the village: ripe, honeyed Spätlese that lives for decades.

places.name: Middle Nahe
places.note: From Schlossböckelheim down to Bad Kreuznach, the valley's grand crus on volcanic rock: porphyry and melaphyre that give smoky, austere, long lived Riesling.

places.name: Schlossböckelheim
places.note: The Kupfergrube, the copper mine, cleared from 1902 by the Prussian state domaine on a worked out mine, porphyry on a steep south face: the most austere and longest lived dry Riesling of the valley; the Felsenberg, volcanic and steep, beside it, and the Königsfels.

places.name: Oberhausen
places.note: The Brücke, a small site on the river bank below the bridge, where the mists give Auslese and the frost gives Eiswein in many winters; the Leistenberg on the slope above.

places.name: Niederhausen
places.note: The Hermannshöhle, the Nahe's most complete site, porphyry and slate on a south face giving Riesling with everything; Hermannsberg, Klamm, Kertz and Steinberg beside it, and the old state domaine's buildings below.

places.name: Norheim
places.note: Dellchen and Kirschheck, small volcanic sites of great finesse on the bend below Niederhausen.

places.name: Traisen
places.note: The Bastei, a scree of porphyry at the foot of the Rotenfels cliff and among the valley's warmest sites: ripe, smoky Riesling; the Rotenfels vineyard above.

places.name: Bockenau
places.note: A side valley west of Bad Kreuznach: the Felseneck, slate and quartzite, taut, smoky and among the valley's best dry Riesling.

places.name: Bad Kreuznach
places.note: The spa town and the valley's capital: Kahlenberg, Krötenpfuhl and Brückes on sandstone and loess give rounder wines, and the trade has its base here.

places.name: Lower Nahe
places.note: From Bad Kreuznach to Bingen the valley opens onto loess, loam and gravel, warmer and nearer the Rheingau in style, with slate and quartzite on the last hills above the Rhine.

places.name: Dorsheim
places.note: Goldloch, Pittermännchen and Burgberg, the lower valley's classified trio: ripe, dense Riesling on slate, quartzite and gravel.

places.name: Münster-Sarmsheim
places.note: Dautenpflänzer and Pittersberg, slate and quartzite near Bingen: firm, dry Riesling and good Pinot.

places.name: Langenlonsheim
places.note: The warm end of the valley: Rothenberg and Löhrer Berg on loess and gravel.

places.name: Rüdesheim an der Nahe
places.note: The village behind the Rosengarten Grosslage; not the Rheingau's Rüdesheim, whatever the label suggests.

producers.name: Dönnhoff
producers.why: Oberhausen; the Brücke, Hermannshöhle, Kupfergrube and Felsenberg from dry GG to Eiswein, the house that put the Nahe on the world's lists.

producers.name: Emrich-Schönleber
producers.why: Monzingen; Halenberg and Frühlingsplätzchen, dry and sweet, the upper valley's standard bearer.

producers.name: Schäfer-Fröhlich
producers.why: Bockenau; Felseneck, Kupfergrube and Felsenberg, wild yeast and long lees, smoky, intense dry Riesling.

producers.name: Weingut Hexamer
producers.why: Meddersheim; the Rheingrafenberg from old vines, long ageing Spätlese, Auslese and Eiswein.

producers.name: Gut Hermannsberg
producers.why: Niederhausen; the former Prussian state domaine of 1902, Kupfergrube and Hermannsberg in dry and sweet styles.

producers.name: Schlossgut Diel
producers.why: Burg Layen; Dorsheim's Goldloch, Pittermännchen and Burgberg, and serious Sekt.

producers.name: Kruger-Rumpf
producers.why: Münster-Sarmsheim; the lower valley's dry Riesling and Pinot from Dautenpflänzer and Pittersberg.

producers.name: Dr. Crusius
producers.why: Traisen; the Bastei beneath the Rotenfels and the Norheim sites.

exam: Place the Nahe: a Rhine tributary meeting it at Bingen, between the Mosel and the Rheingau in both geography and taste.
Carry the soil story: slate, porphyry, sandstone and loess within fifty kilometres, and the wine each gives.
Name three middle valley sites with their villages: Schlossböckelheimer Kupfergrube, Niederhäuser Hermannshöhle, Oberhäuser Brücke.
Know Riesling's share, a little under a third, and the Pinots, Müller-Thurgau and Dornfelder that fill the rest.
For Advanced: the 1902 state domaine, the 1971 law, the single Bereich and the Grosslage names.
traps: The Nahe is not a Mosel tributary; it is the Rhine's, and its wines are fuller than the Saar's and leaner than the Rheingau's.
Oberhausen and Niederhausen are neighbours: the Brücke belongs to Oberhausen, the Hermannshöhle to Niederhausen.
Rüdesheimer Rosengarten is Nahe, not Rheingau.
Schlossböckelheimer Burgweg is a Grosslage; Schlossböckelheimer Kupfergrube is the single site.
Riesling is under a third of the Nahe's vines, not the majority; Müller-Thurgau, Dornfelder and the Pinots together outnumber it.

cards.b: A small valley between Mosel and Rheingau in place and style: Riesling on slate, quartzite and volcanic porphyry, taut, smoky, mineral; dry and sweet alike.

Schlossböckelheimer Kupfergrube and Felsenberg, Niederhäuser Hermannshöhle, Oberhäuser Brücke, Traiser Bastei, Norheimer Dellchen, Monzinger Halenberg and Frühlingsplätzchen, Bockenauer Felseneck, Dorsheimer Goldloch.
Upper (Monzingen, Meddersheim: slate, cool); middle (Schlossböckelheim to Bad Kreuznach: porphyry, the grand crus); lower (Dorsheim, Münster-Sarmsheim: loess, warmer, towards Bingen).
The copper mine: a vineyard at Schlossböckelheim cleared from 1902 by the Prussian state domaine on an old mine; porphyry; the Nahe's most austere, longest lived dry Riesling.
Rüdesheimer Rosengarten is a Nahe Grosslage from Rüdesheim an der Nahe; the Rheingau's Rüdesheim gives Berg Schlossberg. Check the region on the label.
Slate and quartzite (upper), porphyry and melaphyre (middle), sandstone and loess (Bad Kreuznach), loess and gravel (lower): the most varied region in Germany.
Sold as Rhine wine for centuries; the 1971 wine law made it an Anbaugebiet of its own, with one Bereich, Nahetal.

questions.q: Into which river does the Nahe flow?
questions.exp: The Nahe comes down from the hills beyond Idar-Oberstein and meets the Rhine at Bingen, opposite the western end of the Rheingau; the Saar and the Ruwer are the Mosel's tributaries.

questions.q: Which Nahe village gives its name to the Hermannshöhle vineyard?
questions.exp: The Niederhäuser Hermannshöhle is the middle valley's most complete site on porphyry and slate; its neighbour Oberhausen holds the Brücke.

questions.q: The Kupfergrube vineyard at Schlossböckelheim was cleared on the site of what?
questions.exp: Kupfergrube means copper mine: the Prussian state domaine founded in 1902 cleared the worked out mine and the scrub above it into terraces of porphyry.

questions.q: Which rock underlies the Hermannshöhle, the Kupfergrube and the Bastei?
questions.exp: The middle Nahe's grand crus sit on volcanic porphyry and melaphyre; slate rules the upper valley at Monzingen, loess the lower valley, and Muschelkalk belongs to Franken and the Obermosel.

questions.q: In which year did the wine law make the Nahe an Anbaugebiet in its own right?
questions.exp: The 1971 German wine law drew the regions as they stand and gave the Nahe, long sold as Rhine wine, its own name and its single Bereich, Nahetal.

questions.q: Roughly what share of the Nahe's vineyard is planted to Riesling?
questions.exp: Riesling is a little under a third of the Nahe's vines and carries all its fame; Müller-Thurgau, Dornfelder and the Pinots together outnumber it, and four fifths is the Rheingau's Riesling share.

questions.q: To which region does the Grosslage Rüdesheimer Rosengarten belong?
questions.exp: Rüdesheimer Rosengarten is a Nahe Grosslage around Rüdesheim an der Nahe; the Rheingau's Rüdesheim gives the Berg Schlossberg and is a different town.

questions.q: What is the single Bereich of the Nahe?
questions.exp: The whole region from Martinstein to Bingen is one Bereich, Nahetal; under the 2021 law a Bereich is labelled as a Region.
